original_value: AbstractOne form of educational inequality is the disparity that exists between urban and rural settings. Equal distribution of quality education is a challenge for developing countries due to the unavailability of resources. Various approaches to equal distribution are distance learning, telecast learning and e‐learning; however, these approaches cannot achieve the desired objectives due to their limitations. This research aimed to investigate the interesting question of whether mobile technology can bring urban and rural settings closer together. A mobile application for learning Urdu grammar was designed to measure the learning gains of fourth‐grade students at two different schools from urban and rural settings. A quantitative technique, the quasi‐experimental pre‐test and post‐test method, was used to measure the effectiveness of the mobile application. The comparison of the students’ performances at the urban and rural schools illustrated the role of mobile technology in mitigating the educational gap. The present study provides evidence that children from different social backgrounds may benefit equally from mobile technology.

result.paraphrase: One form of educational inequality is the gap between urban and rural settings. In developing countries, the equal distribution of quality education is difficult because resources are unavailable. Distance learning, telecast learning, and e-learning are various attempts to achieve equal distribution, but their limitations prevent them from reaching the desired goals. This research sought to examine whether mobile technology can narrow the divide between urban and rural settings. A mobile app for learning Urdu grammar was developed to assess the learning gains of fourth-grade students at two schools in urban and rural settings. To evaluate the app’s effectiveness, a quantitative quasi-experimental pre-test and post-test method was employed. Comparing student performance at the urban and rural schools showed mobile technology’s role in reducing the educational gap. The study offers evidence that children from different social backgrounds may benefit equally from mobile technology.
